regenerate_when: the taxonomy in ue3_command_suite.py changes, or a new map file appears in local/maps
what_this_is: One entry per kind of command a Legendary Edition build exposes, grouped by the MECHANISM used to reach it. 'present' is measured from local/maps/<game>.json (decompressed identifier tables), never typed by hand; `verify` recomputes it and fails on drift.
evidence_level: present = the identifier exists in that build's decompressed script data. It does NOT prove the function is reachable, owned by the class we intend, or safe to call. `probe` answers those live.

categories.console: Engine exec / console verbs. The one channel that exists in all three builds and needs no code, which makes it the reference implementation for every other command: if a console verb works for player 2 but a direct call does not, the difference is the path, not the engine.
categories.kismet: Sequence (Kismet) objects and their activation. Map events fire from here, and this is where 'the door opened for player 1 and player 2 walked into the back of it' comes from.
categories.pawn: Creating, possessing and releasing a body. The whole point of a second player.
categories.transform: Moving, attaching, hiding, colliding. Cheap to verify and the most common source of a client that is playing a different game.
categories.state: State machine entry and exit. A state a client enters and the host does not is a permanent divergence with no error message.
categories.input: Whether input reaches the pawn, and who it is routed to.
categories.combat: Firing, powers, damage. The player-visible half of the game and the half most likely to be gated per-pawn rather than per-client.
categories.conversation: Dialogue ownership. Player 2 has to become a spectator here without leaving the level.
categories.camera: View target and camera mode. Two clients, two viewports, one set of SetViewTarget calls written for one.
categories.timer: Timers and their identity. A timer set on the host's pawn and read on the client's is a different timer.
categories.save: Save and load. A co-op session that saves half a world is worse than one that refuses.
categories.hud: HUD presence and ownership. Cheap proxy for 'is this client still being rendered as a player'.
categories.replication: Actor roles and the client/server function family. LE3 is the only build with a real replication layer, which is why LE3 goes first.
categories.message: Text to a player. The first thing that breaks when there are two of them and the code says 'the player'.
categories.travel: Level transitions. Every one of them is a place a second client gets dropped.
categories.query: Read-only identity and context lookups. Must all succeed on both clients before any mutating command means anything.
categories.audio: Sound and music. One engine, two listeners; per-player audio is a later problem but the trigger path is the same one as everything else.
categories.anim: Animation and morph control. Scripted animation that assumes the player pawn is the one the script is driving.
categories.pause: Pausing and `bPlayersOnly`. The mechanism that already freezes both players, so it is the one place where a naive implementation looks correct.
categories.squad: Party membership. The client IS a squadmate, so these calls run on the thing the client is trying to control.

risk_levels.high: creates/destroys objects, changes level, touches shared save state
risk_levels.blocked: measured to crash this build; listed so it is not retried

commands.sync: Issue the same console line on both clients and compare what changed; a verb that changes only the caller's world is a desync the console can prove in seconds.
commands.why: The only command channel present in all three builds with no injected code. Every other route in this catalogue has to reproduce what this one already does.

commands.sync: Confirms the console object exists and is reachable, which is what the exec path needs before a line can be delivered.
commands.why: The console state object. Present in LE2/LE3 and absent in LE1, which is a real difference in how a line reaches the engine.

commands.sync: Intercept point: if the hook fires on both clients for one issued line, command delivery is shared and every console-driven test becomes a sync test.
commands.why: A hook callback, ME3 only. Useful as an observation point rather than a call.

commands.sync: The lower-level entry the console verb table dispatches through; distinguishes 'the verb refused' from 'the line never arrived'.
commands.why: Separate from ConsoleCommand in every build, so testing one does not test the other.

commands.sync: Toggles invulnerability on the LOCAL controller only in a naive implementation; a co-op build must decide whether that is per-player or per-world.
commands.why: The clearest example of a verb that is conceptually per-player and is implemented per-controller.

commands.sync: Sets collision off and physics to flying; a client that ghosts its own pawn and not the host's is the classic asymmetric cheat and the classic desync.
commands.why: Combines the collision and physics paths in one verb, so it tests two entries at once.

commands.sync: Changes pawn physics mode. Physics is replicated in LE3 and not in LE1/LE2, so the same verb produces different sync behaviour per game - worth measuring once.
commands.why: Physics-mode change via console. The measured value is visible in the pawn's Physics byte, so this is verifiable without trusting either client's log.

commands.sync: The inverse of Fly; the pair is a round-trip test that leaves the pawn in its original physics mode.
commands.why: Round-trip partner for Fly. Always run both, then assert the physics byte is back.

commands.sync: Reports whether the current level finished loading. The first question to ask a client that is behaving as if the level is not there.
commands.why: A ready flag, not a command. Cheap gate before any level-dependent test.

commands.sync: Time dilation is world state; if it is applied per-client the two clients run at different speeds and every timestamp-based check lies.
commands.why: Directly changes the world's time scale, which is exactly the quantity a naive lockstep implementation assumes is shared.

commands.sync: The same quantity as Slomo but through a property-set path present in LE1, so it gives a third game a way to test time scale.
commands.why: Present in all three builds while Slomo is not, so it is the portable form.

commands.sync: Freezes rendering without stopping the simulation - a state that is easy to mistake for a pause and will be mistaken for one during testing.
commands.why: Separates 'not rendering' from 'not simulating', which a pause test must not conflate.

commands.sync: Freezes every pawn in the level for everyone. Whether player 2 counts as a player here is the question, and it is measurable: the pawn's Physics byte changes.
commands.why: The world-level freeze that conversations and cutscenes already rely on, and the reason a conversation looks 'handled' when it is not.

commands.sync: Kills every pawn in the level. Use on a throwaway copy only; it is the fastest way to prove which pawns a client still counts as alive.
commands.why: Bulk state change with a visible, countable result, so it makes a good assertion target even though it is destructive.

commands.sync: Gives the inventory set. A client that receives the weapons but cannot use them separates inventory sync from input and gate problems.
commands.why: Distinguishes 'the client has the item' from 'the client may use the item', which are different bugs with the same symptom.

commands.sync: Kills the caller's own pawn. The cheapest way to test death and respawn ownership, which is where a second player most often ends up stuck as a spectator.
commands.why: Forces the death path on demand instead of waiting for combat.

commands.sync: Toggles the perf overlay. Harmless and a reliable positive control: if this does not change the screen, the console route is broken and nothing else in the run counts.
commands.why: A positive control. Every suite needs one command that must visibly work.

commands.sync: Reports/toggles physics debug. Read-mostly and present everywhere, so it doubles as a three-game control.
commands.why: Debug rendering path, present in all three, safe for control runs.

commands.sync: Toggles collision debug draw. The visual form of what the collision commands change.
commands.why: Turns a boolean into something a screenshot can prove.

commands.sync: Text to other players. Used for timing markers: both clients log the same string at the same moment, which is the cheapest cross-client clock.
commands.why: A message channel that already exists. Markers sent through it give logs a shared reference without inventing a protocol.

commands.sync: Team index change. In a one-player build this is meaningless, which is exactly why it is worth knowing whether the plumbing is there.
commands.why: Present only where the engine kept team support, so it is a cheap probe of how much multiplayer machinery survived into the single-player build.

commands.sync: Travels to a map. Every level transition is a place a second client is dropped, so this is the transition test itself.
commands.why: The level-transition primitive. Present in all three, so transitions can be tested identically across games.

commands.sync: The login path that ME3SquadCoop's working co-op uses instead of CreatePlayer: it brings up the engine's own multi-player plumbing, which LE1/LE2 never load.
commands.why: For LE3 this is the documented route to a second player. For LE1/LE2 the same verb exists but there is no netcode behind it, so it must not be assumed equivalent.

commands.sync: The inverse of Login; needed to test a session that ends cleanly, which is where half-written co-op mods leave the engine.
commands.why: Every login test needs a logout or the copy must be restarted.

commands.sync: The level's sequence container. Counting sequences on both clients tells you whether both loaded the same Kismet graph, which is upstream of every event divergence.
commands.why: The container for all map events. If the graphs differ, nothing downstream can match.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: Base class of every action and event. Reading its links is what makes it possible to name an event that fires on one client only.
commands.why: Common base for actions and events; its input/output link arrays are the graph.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: Activates a sequence object remotely. This is the command that makes 'delay this until player 2 arrives' possible without editing the level.
commands.why: Remote activation of a Kismet object, present in LE2/LE3. In LE1 the same effect needs TriggerEvent/CauseEvent.

commands.sync: Fires one specific output link instead of the whole action, so a door can be held open for player 2 without re-running the trigger.
commands.why: Finer-grained than Activate: it selects a link, which is what a per-player delay actually needs.

commands.sync: The inbound edges of an action. Reading them tells you which event would have to be held back to delay this action.
commands.why: Graph structure, readable offline in principle and live right now.

commands.sync: The outbound edges. An action with two output links can usually be split so one branch waits.
commands.why: Graph structure again; the split point for a delayed event.

commands.sync: Whether the action is currently running. The direct measurement for 'did this fire on both clients'.
commands.why: The state bit to compare after triggering. Cheap and unambiguous.

commands.sync: Whether the action ever fired at all. Different from bActive, which can be true again after a restart.
commands.why: Latches the 'has run' question, which bActive does not.

commands.sync: The used-flag on events that must only fire once. The exact flag that makes a map event fire for player 1 and be spent before player 2 walks in.
commands.why: This is the flag to inspect when a trigger 'already happened'. Naming it is most of the diagnosis.

commands.sync: A map-level teleport. Whether it moves the acting client only or both is the whole question for any level that moves the player by Kismet.
commands.why: Player movement expressed as level data rather than code, so it exercises the Kismet-to-actor path.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: Matinee playback. Scripted camera and animation is where a second viewer is most obviously in the wrong place.
commands.why: The cutscene driver. Conversations and scripted sequences both route through it.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: A built-in delay node. If the level already has one, delaying for player 2 costs a parameter change rather than new code.
commands.why: Present in LE1/LE2 and absent in LE3, which is itself worth knowing before designing a delay that assumes it.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: The level's own way into cinematic mode. Same effect as the code path, so a client that behaves differently under one and not the other is a client-path bug.
commands.why: Two routes to one state is a useful A/B, and it is how the game actually enters cutscenes.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: Sets a pawn's physics from level data. The documented working placement sequence needs physics 1 before ClientSetLocation, and this is the level-data form of that.
commands.why: Ties the placement order that is already proven to a Kismet action, so a level can reproduce it.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: Fires a named remote event. The portability answer for delayed triggers: all three builds have it, so one mechanism covers all three games.
commands.why: Present everywhere, which makes it the safest cross-game hook for 'player 2 has arrived'.

commands.sync: The older named-event entry. Coexists with CauseEvent in all three, so both should be measured rather than one assumed to subsume the other.
commands.why: A second spelling of the same idea. Present in every build; whether it reaches the same handlers is measurable.

commands.sync: Explicitly remote activation, absent in LE1. Where it exists it is the intended route rather than a side effect.
commands.why: Named for what a co-op trigger needs. Its absence in LE1 is why LE1 needs a different mechanism.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: Creates an actor. Present in all three, which means a second body can be created everywhere; what differs is what the created actor needs attached.
commands.why: The generic creation primitive. It works in all three builds - the failures were always in what a PlayerController needs afterwards, not in Spawn itself.

commands.sync: The GameInfo path that spawns a pawn FOR a controller, including the default pawn class and start spot. This is the call a CreatePlayer would have made internally.
commands.why: Presents in all three. If a second player can be given a body without CreatePlayer, this is where that happens - it takes a controller, so it needs one first.

commands.sync: Respawns a controller's pawn using the normal game rules. The natural way to give an existing second controller a body after death or after a level change.
commands.why: Already the respawn path, so it is exercised by the game itself and less likely to hit an untested branch than a hand-built spawn.

commands.sync: Points a controller at a body. The ME3SquadCoop takeover is exactly this: possess a squadmate pawn. Present in all three, so the mechanism ports.
commands.why: The proven co-op route in LE3. Everything else in this catalogue assumes it worked.

commands.sync: Releases a pawn. Needed to test takeover reversibility; a takeover that cannot be undone is a bug that only shows up when the second player leaves.
commands.why: The inverse of the working route, and the thing to call between test phases so one phase cannot contaminate the next.

commands.sync: Spawns by class name, which is what Kismet and mods use. Absent in LE3, where Spawn(default) is the route.
commands.why: The class-name form a mod would call. Present in LE1/LE2, so those two can create a second body by name.

commands.sync: A debug spawn entry in LE1 only. Worth knowing about because it exists precisely to create actors from a console, which is the fastest experiment loop.
commands.why: LE1-only debug path. Useful, and only in the game that has the fewest alternatives.

commands.sync: The UE3 call that would create a second local player outright. It is present only in LE3, where it works, and measured to crash LE1 and LE2 in three distinct ways.
commands.why: The obvious answer and the wrong one for two of three games. Listed so it is not re-attempted: see CO-OP-FAIL-POINTS.md for the three crash signatures.
commands.note: ME1/LE2 each crashed three ways: ucrtbase!aligned_realloc during the call, an engine-thread fault at +0x99611a AFTER a successful return, and a null PlayerInput call at [rax+0x6D0]. Do not retry without a new mechanism.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: The inverse of CreatePlayer, ME3 only. If a session can be created and not removed, every test needs a restart.
commands.why: Every CreatePlayer test in LE3 needs this to leave a clean process.
commands.role_meaning: the GameViewportClient (players, split layout, HUD class)

commands.sync: Recomputes split-screen layout, which is where the split-screen harness gets its two viewports. The value is a layout enum, and a wrong value silently keeps one pane.
commands.why: Directly controls whether two viewports exist, which is the prerequisite for a local two-player proof before any network work.
commands.role_meaning: the GameViewportClient (players, split layout, HUD class)

commands.sync: The engine's own new-player hook. Calling it by hand exercises exactly what CreatePlayer would have called, with the option to attach things before it runs.
commands.why: Reaching past CreatePlayer to the hook it delegates to is the remaining unproven route, and this catalogues it as such.

commands.sync: The base teleport. Measured to fail on a falling pawn and to work after collisions and physics are corrected, so the ORDER is the finding, not the call.
commands.why: Documented result: Actor.SetLocation alone did not move a falling pawn (z went the wrong way), while SetCollision -> SeqAct_SetPhysics(1) -> ClientSetLocation did.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Rotation follows location. A client that is in the right place facing the wrong way is a camera or a replication problem, and this separates them.
commands.why: Tests rotation independently of position so the two failures are distinguishable.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The replicated form, ME3 only. Its existence in LE3 and absence in LE1/LE2 is the clearest evidence of how much more of the replication layer LE3 kept.
commands.why: The call that actually worked for placement. Present only where a client exists.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Rotation-only replicated form, absent in LE1. Same argument as ClientSetLocation.
commands.why: Completes the replicated pair in LE2/LE3.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: A higher-level teleport that preserves velocity and physics handling. Present where the engine kept it; absent in LE1.
commands.why: Often a better answer than SetLocation for a pawn, because it resolves the physics problem rather than requiring the caller to.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Attaches a pawn to a moving base. On a moving platform, host and client disagree about position by however far the platform moved.
commands.why: Present everywhere, and the mechanism behind every 'the elevator left without me'.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The rigid form of SetBase. Hard attach makes the pawn part of the base, which is right for a vehicle and wrong for anything that should walk off.
commands.why: Distinguishes a soft from a hard attachment, which behave differently across a network boundary.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Hides an actor. The cheapest round-trip test in the catalogue: toggle, read bHidden, toggle back, assert identical.
commands.why: Self-restoring and visible. A positive control for the whole dispatch path.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Scale. A client that applied scale twice looks like a collision bug and is not.
commands.why: Cheap to read back via the scale property, so it verifies numerically.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The portable spelling of scale, in all three builds.
commands.why: Gives LE1 the same test SetDrawScale gives the other two.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The call that has to succeed before a pawn can be placed. Measured as the first step of the working placement order.
commands.why: Proven necessary. Present in LE1/LE2 and replaced by SetCollisionType in LE3.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: LE3's replacement for SetCollision. A port that calls SetCollision on LE3 silently does nothing, which is exactly the class of failure this catalogue is for.
commands.why: Same job, different name. The rename is the porting work.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The state bit SetCollision changes. Read it to verify, rather than trusting the call.
commands.why: Turns a command into an observable, which is what makes the test real.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Enters a stacked state. A state a client enters and the host does not is a permanent divergence with no error.
commands.why: Present in all three. State divergence is silent, so it has to be measured rather than observed.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Leaves the stacked state. The inverse, needed to make a state test repeatable.
commands.why: Round-trip partner for PushState.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The state entry callback. Firing it directly is a way to exercise state logic without a transition.
commands.why: Calling the callback tests the state body without needing a legal transition.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The state exit callback, and the inverse of BeginState.
commands.why: Confirms that whatever BeginState set up can be torn down.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Reports the current state name. THE assertion for every state test: compare the name on both clients, not a guess about what should have happened.
commands.why: Gives state divergence a comparable value.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The input object on a controller. LE1 crashed with a NULL PlayerInput when spawning a controller, so this pointer is the thing a second player is missing.
commands.why: Measured null on a hand-built controller, and the crash followed. Read it first.

commands.sync: Pushes the PC bindings into a controller's input. The step that turns a created input object into one that responds to keys.
commands.why: Present in all three. Runs after PlayerInput exists, and is the safe half of input setup.

commands.sync: Grants an actor input processing. LE3 only, so input gating is expressible in LE3 and must be done another way in LE1/LE2.
commands.why: The explicit gate. Its absence in LE1/LE2 is a real capability difference.

commands.sync: The inverse gate, and the mechanism a spectator mode would use.
commands.why: Reverses EnableInput; needed so a spectator can be un-spectated.

commands.sync: The code path into the same state ToggleCinematicMode reaches from level data. Measured to be present in all three, so a spectator lock can be built on it.
commands.why: The control hook with the widest availability. Sets bCinematicMode, which is readable, so the effect is verifiable.

commands.sync: The bit SetCinematicMode writes. The assertion, not the command.
commands.why: Readable in all three, so the effect of the command can be proved.

commands.sync: ME1's own Kismet action for changing which pawn the player controls. This is the closest thing LE1 has to a built-in takeover.
commands.why: The single most promising LE1-specific hook found. Present in LE1 only, and it is a level-data command, so it needs no injected code to try.

commands.sync: An ME1 Kismet event that fires on player input. An existing per-input observation point, which a spectator mode would need.
commands.why: LE1-only observation hook. Useful for logging what player 1 did, in order.

commands.sync: ME1's input trap: a level-data way to stop the player acting for a while. The closest existing analogue to a control gate.
commands.why: LE1-only. It is the game's own 'the player cannot act here', which is the semantic a spectator needs.

commands.sync: The gate. Present in all three, which makes it the first thing to read on a pawn the client is supposed to control.
commands.why: Documented as the function that decides whether firing is allowed. If it is false on a squadmate, possession alone does not produce a working client.

commands.sync: Begins firing. Present everywhere, so a second player's ability to shoot can be tested in all three games.
commands.why: The player-visible half of the game. A silent no-op here is the bug the whole project is about.

commands.sync: Ends firing. Absent in LE1, so LE1's fire loop must be closed another way.
commands.why: Round-trip partner, and a real per-game difference.

commands.sync: ME3's differently-named gate. A port that calls CanFireWeapon on LE3 may be reading a different answer.
commands.why: The rename that matters. Two similar names, only one is live per build.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The ME3 internal fire path. It is where a client-only fire decision would be made if one exists.
commands.why: Documented in the firing chain notes as the ME3 route, hence worth naming separately.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: LE1's spelling of the fire event. The third spelling across three builds, which is the point: one concept, three names.
commands.why: Names must be resolved per build, not assumed.

commands.sync: A second fire spelling in LE2/LE3. Coexists with StartFire, so both should be measured.
commands.why: Two plausible entry points in the same build means guessing is unsafe.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Uses a power by id. Powers are the most per-pawn-gated action after firing, and the easiest to make silent.
commands.why: Present in all three, so power gating can be tested identically across games.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The ability-level form. Present everywhere, distinct from UsePower in the same builds.
commands.why: A second power path in all three: measuring one does not measure the other.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Explicit activation rather than use. Present in all three.
commands.why: Completes the trio; a port that maps only one of three names leaves two paths dead.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The hotkey route into powers, i.e. the input-driven one. A power that works via UsePower and not via doHotKey has an input problem, not a power problem.
commands.why: Separates the power path from the input path, which are otherwise conflated.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Orders a squadmate to use a power. THIS is the command a client playing a squadmate collides with: the host is already issuing it.
commands.why: Present in all three and directly about squad AI, so a co-op client fights it for control of the same pawn.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Damage entry. Whether a client's pawn is damageable decides whether combat is authoritative on one machine or two.
commands.why: Present everywhere. The single call that decides if the client's squadmate is invulnerable or doubly damageable.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The caller side of damage. Absent in LE1, so LE1 tests must use TakeDamage.
commands.why: Shows the asymmetry: the same concept has different names for caller and callee per build.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Puts the pawn in a busy state, which blocks actions. One of the fewer-known gates that leaves the player unable to shoot with no obvious cause.
commands.why: Absent in LE3, present in LE1/LE2. A gate that exists in two builds and not the third, and is invisible unless measured.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Adds a weapon. ME3 only; LE1/LE2 use AddInventory.
commands.why: Weapon ownership has three different entry points across three builds.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The LE2/LE3 inventory route. Distinct from GiveWeapon even where both exist.
commands.why: Same outcome, different path; a port must not assume one implies the other.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Starts dialogue. Absent in LE3, so LE3's conversation entry is elsewhere and must not be assumed identical.
commands.why: The obvious hook, present in two of three builds. The winner of a conversation does not need it, but the loser does.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Ends dialogue and returns control. Where a spectator must be un-spectated.
commands.why: The inverse, and the point where a client most often stays stuck in a cinematic camera.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: LE3's conversation state. The readable form of 'a conversation owns the player'.
commands.why: Gives LE3 the same assertion the conversation detector provides live.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Facial animation from a name. LE1 only; it is how dialogue is lip-synced there.
commands.why: LE1-only, and it is the visible sign of a conversation, so it doubles as an observation point.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Chooses what a client looks at. With two clients this is the call that must become per-player, and getting it wrong makes the second player's screen unusable.
commands.why: Present in LE1/LE3. Directly controls the second viewport's contents.

commands.sync: The replicated form. Its presence only in LE1 and LE3 is another per-game split.
commands.why: The form that would actually be used over a network.

commands.sync: Camera mode selection. Present in all three, so the second player's camera mode is expressible everywhere.
commands.why: The portable camera lever.

commands.sync: Reads the current view. The assertion for every camera test: compare the two clients' reported viewpoints rather than guessing.
commands.why: Present in all three and gives a comparable value.

commands.sync: The per-frame camera update. ME3 only; useful as a hook point for a second camera.
commands.why: Where a second viewport's camera would be driven.

commands.sync: Computes the camera position for one controller. The function a second viewport needs to be called for it.
commands.why: ME3-only. Naming it is the first step to calling it twice.

commands.sync: Sets a named timer. Timers are keyed by name AND function, so a timer set on one object is invisible to another with the same name.
commands.why: Present everywhere. A cheap, verifiable round-trip and a real trap for anything that assumes timers are global.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Clears the named timer. The inverse.
commands.why: Round-trip partner; without it a timer test leaves a callback firing.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Whether the timer exists. The assertion, and it distinguishes 'never set' from 'already fired'.
commands.why: The observable that makes a timer test real.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Writes a save. A co-op session that saves one player's world is worse than one that refuses, so the behaviour has to be known before it is allowed.
commands.why: Present in all three, and the save system is shared between copies through a fixed Documents path - so this is a real hazard during testing, not a hypothetical.

commands.sync: Loads a save, i.e. tears down and rebuilds the world. The most destructive command in the catalogue.
commands.why: Needs a restore point and a throwaway copy. Listed so it is used deliberately.

commands.sync: Writes the profile. Shared across every copy on the machine, so a test that runs it changes player 1's real profile.
commands.why: The sharpest shared-state hazard in the whole test environment.

commands.sync: Whether saving is currently legal. The gate to read before considering a save test.
commands.why: Absent in LE1, so LE1 has no safe way to ask first.

commands.sync: Shows or hides the HUD. A reliable, visible per-client effect, so it is the cheapest proof that a command reached a specific client.
commands.why: Two clients have two HUDs, so this is the clearest 'did it arrive' signal.

commands.sync: The inverse toggle, ME3 only.
commands.why: Completes the HUD pair where it exists.

commands.sync: Replaces a client's HUD class. The replicated form, and the one a second viewport would need a distinct instance of.
commands.why: ME3-only. Named for the client, which is exactly the distinction that matters here.

commands.sync: An actor's authority role. The single field that says whether a client's copy is allowed to act, and it exists in all three builds even though only LE3 has netcode.
commands.why: Readable everywhere. In LE1/LE2 it is vestigial, which is itself worth measuring rather than assuming.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The other end's role. Absent in LE1, so LE1 cannot express an asymmetric authority.
commands.why: A per-game capability difference with a clean observable.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Whether the local player owns this actor. The exact question a co-op client is asking about the squadmate it is controlling.
commands.why: ME3-only, and it is the engine's own answer to 'who may act on this'.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: How often an actor replicates. ME3 only; the tuning knob for a second player's smoothness.
commands.why: Only meaningful where a replication layer exists, i.e. LE3.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The replicated-property notification. Calling it by hand simulates a replicate that never arrived, which is the cheapest way to test the notification path.
commands.why: ME3-only. Turns 'what happens on a late replicate' into a testable call.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The movement RPC a client sends to the server. Named here because it is the exact route a second client's movement would take if the engine path were used.
commands.why: ME3-only. 198 of the 283 client/server-shaped names live only in LE3, and this is the one that matters most.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The server's acknowledgement of a client move. The other half of ServerMove.
commands.why: Together with ServerMove it is the engine's own movement sync, which is what a hand-built co-op would otherwise reimplement.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Server correction of a client position. The mechanism that resolves a client's disagreement about where it is.
commands.why: The correction pass. Relevant to any desync where positions drift but movement works.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Text to the local player. Present in all three, so it works as a marker channel in every build.
commands.why: A per-client message that cannot affect state, which makes it a safe cross-client timing marker.

commands.sync: Localized text to all players. Absent in LE1, where the localized path is different.
commands.why: Another per-game split in a subsystem a co-op mod will want for its own UI.

commands.sync: LE3's message route, distinct from ClientMessage in the same build.
commands.why: Two message paths in one build is exactly why names must be resolved, not assumed.

commands.sync: The receiving end of the localized path.
commands.why: Completes the pair so a message test can assert receipt, not just send.

commands.sync: Changes the level for everyone. The mechanism a co-op session would use to keep two clients together, and the one that drops a client when it fails.
commands.why: Absent in LE1, so LE1 transitions are all local. Another capability difference that changes the design per game.

commands.sync: Sends one client to a URL. The per-client half of a transition.
commands.why: ME3-only. The call that would let the client follow the host.

commands.sync: ME3 console-level map change. Distinct from ServerTravel in the same build.
commands.why: A third transition spelling, all in LE3.

commands.sync: Switches level without a full travel. ME3 only.
commands.why: The cheap transition, useful for a test area that needs a reset without a reload.

commands.sync: Restarts the current level. ME3 only; the cleanest way to reset a test phase.
commands.why: A reset that does not need a process restart, which is the expensive thing here.

commands.sync: Whether this controller is locally controlled. For a co-op client the answer should become true for the second player, and it is the single best gate before any input or camera test.
commands.why: Absent in LE2, present in LE1/LE3. The direct answer to 'is this client a player or a spectator'.

commands.sync: Returns a local player controller. Note the 'A': it returns an arbitrary one, which in a two-player build is exactly the ambiguity this project is about.
commands.why: Present in LE1/LE3. A function whose name promises less than a caller assumes.

commands.sync: Controller by index. Present in all three, so 'which player am I' is expressible everywhere.
commands.why: The portable way to address player 2 rather than 'the' player.

commands.sync: Pawn by index. ME3 only, so LE1/LE2 must go through the controller.
commands.why: A convenience that only one build has; a port must not rely on it.

commands.sync: The class of a local controller. Present in all three, so type checks are portable.
commands.why: Useful to verify that a hand-built controller is the class the rest of the code expects.
commands.role_meaning: no specific instance: a class-level lookup, or a Kismet action the game side must find by name

commands.sync: The current map name. Present in all three and the cheapest way to prove two clients are in the same level.
commands.why: The first assertion of every multi-client test.

commands.sync: A second map-name accessor, absent in LE1.
commands.why: A port that calls only one of the two will fail on one game.

commands.sync: Plays a sound locally. Present in all three, so it is a safe positive control that produces an observable change without touching game state.
commands.why: A control with a visible log line and no state change - rare and useful.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The replicated sound path. ME3 only, and the one that matters once two clients exist.
commands.why: Only meaningful with a client, which is the definition of LE3's advantage.

commands.sync: Silences everything. A blunt reset that is useful when a test leaves audio looping.
commands.why: Cleanup, not a test.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Stops the music track. LE1 only in this spelling.
commands.why: LE1-only audio control; listed because LE1 has the fewest levers.

commands.sync: Plays an animation on a skeletal mesh. Present everywhere, so scripted animation can be exercised in every build.
commands.why: Animation is a common source of a client looking wrong while behaving right.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Stops it. The inverse.
commands.why: Round-trip partner.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: The ME3 actor-level form, distinct from PlayAnim in the same build.
commands.why: A third spelling; measuring one does not measure the other.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Facial morph weight. ME3 only, and the mechanism behind expressions in dialogue.
commands.why: Relevant to a spectator: expression changes are visible to both, so they must be either shared or suppressed.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Swaps a mesh. The most visible possible test of whether a command reached a specific pawn.
commands.why: Present everywhere and unmistakable, which makes it a good end-to-end control.
commands.role_meaning: the local player's pawn (Physics, Location, Firing)

commands.sync: Pauses the game for the caller. In a one-player build this is global; with two clients it has to become per-session or it freezes both.
commands.why: Present in all three. The first command that must change meaning for co-op.

commands.sync: Unpauses. Absent in LE1, so LE1's pause must be closed by SetPause(false).
commands.why: An asymmetry that would leave LE1 stuck if a port assumed ClearPause.

commands.sync: Pauses via the game object rather than a controller.
commands.why: A second pause route; the one that is world-wide by construction.

commands.sync: The world flag that freezes pawns. Readable in all three and the same flag conversations set.
commands.why: The observable that makes 'the world thinks a cutscene is running' measurable.

commands.sync: Adds a squad member. Present everywhere, so the party can be arranged identically across games.
commands.why: The party container is what the client is trying to control, so knowing how it is edited matters.
commands.role_meaning: the squadmate pawn the client is meant to control

commands.sync: Removes one. The inverse.
commands.why: Round-trip partner; also the way to test a client leaving.
commands.role_meaning: the squadmate pawn the client is meant to control

commands.sync: Type/marker for a squad member pawn. The classification a takeover has to recognise.
commands.why: The offline and live way to tell a squadmate from the player, which is the first discrimination a co-op mod needs.
commands.role_meaning: the squadmate pawn the client is meant to control
